sections.title: What you need from earlier units

sections.body:
A **variational** algorithm prepares `ψ(θ)` with a circuit whose gates have
angles `θ = (θ_1, …, θ_m)`, measures the energy `E(θ)`, and adjusts `θ` to
lower it. On hardware, `E(θ)` is never available as a formula: each value
is an average over repeated runs, with a statistical error of order
`1/√(runs)`. Peruzzo and coauthors ran such a variational eigenvalue solver
on a photonic processor.

Gradient descent needs `∂E/∂θ_k`. A central finite difference,
`(E(θ + ε e_k) - E(θ - ε e_k)) / 2ε`, divides the statistical error of
each energy by `2ε`: with `ε = 0.01` an error of `0.001` per energy becomes
0.1 in the gradient. A small `ε` is exactly what a finite difference needs,
and exactly what noise punishes.

The **parameter-shift rule** of the next sections gives the exact gradient
from two energies at angles shifted by `±π/2`, a large step, so the
statistical error is not amplified.

choices: They need each gate's derivative formula
Shot noise in each energy gets divided by the small ε
Hardware cannot run the same circuit twice with different angles
questions.explain: Each energy is a sample mean with an error of order `1/√(runs)`. The difference of two such estimates, divided by `2ε`, has an error of order `1/(ε √runs)`, which grows as `ε` shrinks.
misconceptions: Finite differences need no derivative formula at all; that is their appeal. Their problem is noise amplification.
Changing an angle and rerunning is the basic operation of every variational algorithm; it is what both methods do.
questions.prompt: Why is a finite-difference gradient a poor choice on quantum hardware?

sections.title: The question: how do you compute the gradient of a circuit you can only run?

sections.body:
Hamiltonians are written as sums of **Pauli strings**, products of `I`,
`X`, `Y`, `Z` on each qubit, such as `"ZZ"` or `"XI"`. This unit writes a
string with **character `q + 1` for qubit `q`**, so `"XI"` is `X` on qubit 0,
matching the little-endian order (as a `kron`, it is `I ⊗ X`).

The matrix of an `n`-qubit string has `4^n` entries. It is not needed: a
Pauli string maps each basis state `|k⟩` to a single basis state times a
phase,

```
P |k⟩ = phase(k) |k ⊻ m⟩
```

where `m` has the bits of the qubits with `X` or `Y` (those flip), and
`phase(k)` collects `-1` for each `Z` on a 1 bit, and `i` or `-i` for each
`Y` on a 0 or 1 bit (`Y|0⟩ = i|1⟩`, `Y|1⟩ = -i|0⟩`). Then

```
ψ' P ψ = Σ over k of conj(ψ[(k ⊻ m) + 1]) · phase(k) · ψ[k + 1]
```

which is real for a Hermitian `P`, and costs `O(n 2^n)` with no extra
memory. The energy is a sum of such terms with their coefficients.

examples.caption: `ψ' P ψ` by bit operations against the dense `kron` matrix, for all 16 two-qubit Pauli strings on a random state.
examples.code:
using Random
function pauli_expectation(ψ, s)                   # s[q + 1] is the Pauli on qubit q
    m = 0
    for (i, c) in enumerate(s)
        (c == 'X' || c == 'Y') && (m |= 1 << (i - 1))
    end
    acc = zero(ComplexF64)
    for k in 0:length(ψ)-1
        ph = one(ComplexF64)
        for (i, c) in enumerate(s)
            b = (k >> (i - 1)) & 1
            c == 'Z' && b == 1 && (ph = -ph)
            c == 'Y' && (ph *= b == 0 ? im : -im)
        end
        acc += conj(ψ[(k ⊻ m) + 1]) * ph * ψ[k + 1]
    end
    return real(acc)
end
P = Dict('I' => ComplexF64[1 0; 0 1], 'X' => ComplexF64[0 1; 1 0], 'Y' => ComplexF64[0 -im; im 0], 'Z' => ComplexF64[1 0; 0 -1])
dense(s) = reduce(kron, [P[c] for c in reverse(s)])           # qubit 0 is the rightmost factor
v = randn(Xoshiro(60), ComplexF64, 4); v ./= sqrt(sum(abs2, v))
worst = maximum(abs(pauli_expectation(v, a * b) - real(v' * dense(a * b) * v)) for a in "IXYZ", b in "IXYZ")
println("16 strings: largest difference from the dense matrix below 1e-14: ", worst < 1e-14)
println("dense matrix entries for n = 20: ", 4^20, ",  amplitudes: ", 2^20)
examples.output:
16 strings: largest difference from the dense matrix below 1e-14: true
dense matrix entries for n = 20: 1099511627776,  amplitudes: 1048576

choices: P is diagonal, so only the probabilities matter
P maps each basis state to one other basis state times a phase
The kron product of 2×2 matrices is never actually needed by Julia, which optimises it away
questions.explain: Each column of `P` has a single nonzero entry, so `P ψ` is a permutation of `ψ` with phases. The sum over `k` touches each amplitude once, with `n` bit checks for the phase.
misconceptions: Only strings made of `I` and `Z` are diagonal. `X` and `Y` flip bits, and their expectation values depend on the phases of the amplitudes, not just the probabilities.
Julia forms the `kron` matrix if asked to, with all its `4^n` entries; avoiding it is the algorithm's choice, not the compiler's.
questions.prompt: Why can `ψ' P ψ` for a Pauli string `P` be computed in `O(n 2^n)` time without forming `P`?

sections.title: Pauli strings without their matrices

analogies.breaks:
Real tides are only approximately sinusoidal, and the quarter-period trick
would then be approximate. For a circuit energy as a function of one `RY`
angle it is exact, because the energy is a sum of `1`, `cos θ` and `sin θ`
with nothing else. For gates whose generator has more than two eigenvalues
the rule needs more shifts.
analogies.text:
A tide rises and falls like a sine wave. To know how fast it is rising now,
you could compare the water level a minute ago and a minute from now: a
tiny difference, easily lost in waves. Or, knowing it is a pure sine with a
known period, compare the levels a quarter period before and after, a big
difference, and get the rate now exactly.
analogies.title: Reading the tide from two clocks

sections.body:
Take one gate `RY(θ) = exp(-iθY/2)`. Its matrix entries are `cos(θ/2)` and
`sin(θ/2)`, and the energy is quadratic in them, so with all other angles
fixed

```
E(θ) = a + b cos θ + c sin θ          (since cos²(θ/2) = (1 + cos θ)/2, and so on)
```

for some constants `a`, `b`, `c`. For such a function, two values half a
period apart give the derivative exactly:

```
(E(θ + π/2) - E(θ - π/2)) / 2  =  -b sin θ + c cos θ  =  E'(θ)
```

This is the **parameter-shift rule**, given for gates generated by Pauli
operators by Mitarai et al. and generalised by Schuld et al. It costs two
energy evaluations per angle, like a central difference, but has no step
size to choose and no truncation error, and its large step does not
amplify noise.

diagrams.alt: A sinusoidal curve E of theta over one period. A point at theta has a tangent line. Two further points at theta minus pi/2 and theta plus pi/2 are joined by a dashed chord; the chord's rise divided by 2 equals the slope of the tangent at theta. A small pair of points close to theta, labelled finite difference, has a tiny rise that noise bars swamp.
diagrams.caption: For `E(θ) = a + b cos θ + c sin θ`, the difference of the values at `θ ± π/2`, halved, is exactly the slope at `θ`. A finite difference uses two close points whose small difference is easily lost in measurement noise.

examples.caption: The parameter-shift gradient of a 4-angle two-qubit circuit against central differences with `ε = 1e-6`, at 5 random angle vectors.
examples.code:
using Random
function apply_1q!(ψ, U, q)
    s = 1 << q
    for k in 0:length(ψ)-1
        if k & s == 0
            a, b = ψ[k + 1], ψ[k + s + 1]
            ψ[k + 1], ψ[k + s + 1] = U[1, 1] * a + U[1, 2] * b, U[2, 1] * a + U[2, 2] * b
        end
    end
    return ψ
end
function apply_cx!(ψ, c, t)
    for k in 0:length(ψ)-1
        if k & (1 << c) != 0 && k & (1 << t) == 0
            j = k | (1 << t)
            ψ[k + 1], ψ[j + 1] = ψ[j + 1], ψ[k + 1]
        end
    end
    return ψ
end
RY(θ) = ComplexF64[cos(θ/2) -sin(θ/2); sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2)]
function ansatz(θ)                                   # RY, RY, CX 0→1, RY, RY
    ψ = ComplexF64[1, 0, 0, 0]
    apply_1q!(ψ, RY(θ[1]), 0); apply_1q!(ψ, RY(θ[2]), 1); apply_cx!(ψ, 0, 1)
    apply_1q!(ψ, RY(θ[3]), 0); apply_1q!(ψ, RY(θ[4]), 1)
    return ψ
end
function energy(θ)                                   # ZZ + (X on q0 + X on q1)/2, by bit operations
    ψ = ansatz(θ)
    zz = sum(abs2(ψ[k + 1]) * (isodd(count_ones(k)) ? -1 : 1) for k in 0:3)
    x0 = real(sum(conj(ψ[(k ⊻ 1) + 1]) * ψ[k + 1] for k in 0:3))
    x1 = real(sum(conj(ψ[(k ⊻ 2) + 1]) * ψ[k + 1] for k in 0:3))
    return zz + 0.5 * (x0 + x1)
end
unit(k, m) = [i == k ? 1.0 : 0.0 for i in 1:m]
shift_gradient(f, θ) = [(f(θ + π/2 * unit(k, length(θ))) - f(θ - π/2 * unit(k, length(θ)))) / 2 for k in eachindex(θ)]
fd_gradient(f, θ; ε = 1e-6) = [(f(θ + ε * unit(k, length(θ))) - f(θ - ε * unit(k, length(θ)))) / 2ε for k in eachindex(θ)]
rng = Xoshiro(60)
diff = maximum(maximum(abs.(shift_gradient(energy, θ) - fd_gradient(energy, θ))) for θ in [2π * rand(rng, 4) for _ in 1:5])
println("largest |shift - finite difference|: ", round(diff; sigdigits = 2))
examples.output: largest |shift - finite difference|: 3.6e-10

choices: Below 1e-13: both are exact here
Between 1e-12 and 1e-8: the finite difference's own error
About 1e-3
predict.explain: The shift rule is exact up to a few `eps`. The central difference has a truncation error of order `ε² E''' / 6 ≈ 1e-13` and a rounding error of order `eps · |E| / ε ≈ 1e-10`, which dominates: the measured difference is the finite difference's error. The two methods agree to about 1e-10, which a test can use as its tolerance.
predict.prompt: Both gradients are computed in floating point, without noise. Before the output is shown: how large is the largest difference between them?

choices: π/2 is small enough that higher-order terms vanish
E(θ) is a + b cos θ + c sin θ in each angle
It is not exact, only close
questions.explain: A function with only the frequencies 0 and 1 has its derivative determined by two values half a period apart, at any `θ`. That is a fact about this function class, not a Taylor approximation.
misconceptions: `π/2` is a large step; for a general function it would give a poor estimate. The rule is exact because `E` has no higher frequencies, not because the step is small.
It is exact: the measured difference from finite differences comes from the finite difference's own error, about `1e-10`.
questions.prompt: Why is the shift of `π/2` exact, not an approximation?

sections.title: The parameter-shift rule

sections.body:
Gradient descent with the shift rule, `θ ← θ - 0.2 ∇E(θ)` for 400 steps,
from five random starting angles, reaches the ground energy. By the
variational principle no angle can go below `E0`, which 10 000 random angle
vectors confirm.

**Control.** Remove the CNOT. Then the circuit can only make product
states `RY(b)|0⟩ ⊗ RY(a)|0⟩`, whose energy is
`z_0 z_1 + (x_0 + x_1)/2` with Bloch vectors in the `x`-`z` plane. The best
product state has `x_0 = x_1 = -1/2` and `z_0 = -z_1 = √3/2`, giving
`-3/4 - 1/2 = -1.25`. Since the ground state is entangled (0.60 bits), no
product state reaches `-√2`, and a VQE that passed with this circuit would
point to a bug in the check, not a success.

examples.caption: Gradient descent from 5 random starts, the variational principle on 10 000 random angle vectors, and the product-state control on a 400 × 400 grid.
examples.code:
using Random
function apply_1q!(ψ, U, q)
    s = 1 << q
    for k in 0:length(ψ)-1
        if k & s == 0
            a, b = ψ[k + 1], ψ[k + s + 1]
            ψ[k + 1], ψ[k + s + 1] = U[1, 1] * a + U[1, 2] * b, U[2, 1] * a + U[2, 2] * b
        end
    end
    return ψ
end
function apply_cx!(ψ, c, t)
    for k in 0:length(ψ)-1
        if k & (1 << c) != 0 && k & (1 << t) == 0
            j = k | (1 << t)
            ψ[k + 1], ψ[j + 1] = ψ[j + 1], ψ[k + 1]
        end
    end
    return ψ
end
RY(θ) = ComplexF64[cos(θ/2) -sin(θ/2); sin(θ/2) cos(θ/2)]
function state_energy(ψ)
    zz = sum(abs2(ψ[k + 1]) * (isodd(count_ones(k)) ? -1 : 1) for k in 0:3)
    x0 = real(sum(conj(ψ[(k ⊻ 1) + 1]) * ψ[k + 1] for k in 0:3))
    x1 = real(sum(conj(ψ[(k ⊻ 2) + 1]) * ψ[k + 1] for k in 0:3))
    return zz + 0.5 * (x0 + x1)
end
function ansatz(θ; entangle = true)
    ψ = ComplexF64[1, 0, 0, 0]
    apply_1q!(ψ, RY(θ[1]), 0); apply_1q!(ψ, RY(θ[2]), 1); entangle && apply_cx!(ψ, 0, 1)
    apply_1q!(ψ, RY(θ[3]), 0); apply_1q!(ψ, RY(θ[4]), 1)
    return ψ
end
energy(θ) = state_energy(ansatz(θ))
unit(k, m) = [i == k ? 1.0 : 0.0 for i in 1:m]
shift_gradient(f, θ) = [(f(θ + π/2 * unit(k, length(θ))) - f(θ - π/2 * unit(k, length(θ)))) / 2 for k in eachindex(θ)]
function vqe(f, rng)
    θ = 2π * rand(rng, 4)
    for _ in 1:400
        θ .-= 0.2 * shift_gradient(f, θ)
    end
    return f(θ)
end
rng = Xoshiro(60)
E0 = -sqrt(2)
best = minimum(vqe(energy, rng) for _ in 1:5)
println("VQE best of 5 starts: ", round(best; digits = 10), ",  |best - E0| below 1e-12: ", abs(best - E0) < 1e-12)
println("smallest energy over 10 000 random angles ≥ E0: ", minimum(energy(2π * rand(rng, 4)) for _ in 1:10_000) >= E0 - 1e-12)
product(a, b) = state_energy(kron(RY(b) * ComplexF64[1, 0], RY(a) * ComplexF64[1, 0]))
println("product states, best on the grid: ", round(minimum(product(a, b) for a in range(0, 2π, 400), b in range(0, 2π, 400)); digits = 3))
examples.output:
VQE best of 5 starts: -1.4142135624,  |best - E0| below 1e-12: true
smallest energy over 10 000 random angles ≥ E0: true
product states, best on the grid: -1.25

choices: About -1.25
-1, the ZZ part alone
predict.explain: The best product state has `z_0 z_1 = -3/4` and `(x_0 + x_1)/2 = -1/2`, for `-1.25`. Trading some `ZZ` energy for `X` energy beats -1, but only an entangled state reaches `-√2`. A gap of 0.16 is far larger than the grid's resolution, so the control fails clearly.
predict.prompt: Without the CNOT, the circuit makes only product states. Before the output is shown: what is the lowest energy it reaches on the grid?

choices: Gradient descent got stuck in a local minimum
It has too few parameters: two angles instead of four
The ground state is entangled
questions.explain: Without an entangling gate every reachable state is a product, and the ground state has 0.60 bits of entanglement, so it is out of reach for any angles; -1.25 is the minimum over all product states, found on a grid, not by descent.
misconceptions: The control minimises over a fine grid of every angle pair, not by descent, so there is no local minimum to get stuck in; -1.25 is the global minimum over product states.
More single-qubit angles would not help: any number of them still makes only product states.
questions.prompt: The circuit without the CNOT stops at -1.25, above `E0 = -√2`. Why?

sections.title: VQE reaches -√2; a circuit without entanglement cannot

units.summary: A variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) tunes the angles of a small circuit to minimise an energy. The unit computes expectation values of Pauli strings without forming their 2^n × 2^n matrices, derives the parameter-shift rule (an exact gradient from two shifted runs per angle) and checks it against central differences, reaches the ground energy -√2 of a two-qubit Ising Hamiltonian within 1e-12 from five random starts, and shows with a control that circuits without an entangling gate stop at -1.25.
units.title: Variational algorithms

hints: A global phase multiplies every entry by the same `c`. If you knew `c`, the test is a single comparison; one entry of `a` and `b` is enough to find it, as long as that entry of `b` is not zero.
Take `k = argmax(abs.(b))`, set `c = a[k] / b[k]` and normalise `c /= abs(c)`; return `maximum(abs.(a .- c .* b)) <= 1e-10`. Return `false` first if `a[k]` is tiny.
problems.prompt:
Two state vectors describe the same physical state when they differ by a
global phase `c` with `|c| = 1`. Write `equal_up_to_phase(a, b)` for two
normalised `Vector{ComplexF64}` of the same length that returns `true` if
there is such a `c` with `maximum(abs.(a .- c .* b)) <= 1e-10`, and
`false` otherwise.

```julia
equal_up_to_phase(ComplexF64[1, 1] / sqrt(2), ComplexF64[im, im] / sqrt(2))     # true
equal_up_to_phase(ComplexF64[1, 1] / sqrt(2), ComplexF64[1, -1] / sqrt(2))      # false: a relative phase
```

The generated cases are a phase times `b` plus noise below `1e-14`, or
that with one entry changed (a relative phase of 0.5 rad, or `1e-7` added
and the vector renormalised), or another random state. Some cases have
`b[1] = 0`.
problems.title: Equal up to a global phase

hints: Run the test on each mutant and count the failures. A mutant that makes the test throw is detected too, so the call has to be protected.
Wrap `test(m)` in `try ... catch; false; end`, and count the mutants for which that is not `true`.
problems.prompt:
Write `mutation_score(mutants, test)` that returns how many of the
functions in the vector `mutants` are **killed** by `test`, as an `Int`.
`test(f)` runs a check on the implementation `f` and returns `true` when
it passes. A mutant is killed when `test` returns `false` or throws an
exception (a crash counts as a detected bug).

```julia
test = f -> f(3) == 9
mutation_score([x -> x^2, x -> 3x, x -> x + 6, x -> error("boom")], test)      # 1: only error("boom")
mutation_score([x -> 2x, x -> x^3], f -> f(2) == 4)                             # 1: x -> x^3
```

(In the first example `x -> 3x` and `x -> x + 6` survive, since both give
9 at 3: one test input is a weak suite.)

samples.call: mutation_score([x -> x^2, x -> 3x, x -> x + 6, x -> error("boom")], f -> f(3) == 9)
mutation_score([x -> x, x -> -x, x -> abs(x)], f -> f(-2) == -2 && f(5) == 5)
mutation_score([x -> sqrt(x), x -> x / 0], f -> f(4) == 2.0)

problems.title: Counting killed mutants

hints: First the expected counts `N p[i]` from the total `N`; then the sum of squared differences, each divided by its expected count.
`N = sum(counts)`; for each `i`, `e = N * p[i]`; add `(counts[i] - e)^2 / e`. Start the sum at `0.0` so the result is a `Float64`.
problems.prompt:
Write `chi_square(counts, p)` that returns Pearson's statistic

```
χ² = Σ over i of (counts[i] - N p[i])² / (N p[i]),      N = sum(counts)
```

as a `Float64`, for a `Vector{Int}` of observed counts and a
`Vector{Float64}` of probabilities of the same length, all `p[i] > 0`,
summing to 1.

```julia
chi_square([50, 50], [0.5, 0.5])            # 0.0
chi_square([60, 40], [0.5, 0.5])            # 4.0
chi_square([30, 30, 40], [0.25, 0.25, 0.5]) # 4.0
```

Results are compared with a relative tolerance of `1e-12`: the statistic is
a sum of at most a few hundred positive terms, each computed with a few
roundings.

sections.body:
This unit looks back at the checks of units 49-60 and asks what each one
can and cannot show. It uses `apply_1q!` (unit 52), the CHSH correlator
`E(x, y) = cos(x - y)` for the Bell state (unit 53), `measure!` with
collapse (unit 54), and the phase-estimation readout (unit 58).

**Sampling error.** A frequency estimated from `N` independent shots of an
event with probability `p` has standard deviation `σ = √(p(1 - p)/N)`. The
checks in this course accept a sampled frequency when it lies within `5σ`
of the prediction: a correct sampler fails such a check with probability
below `6e-7`, so a failure points at a bug, not at bad luck.
sections.title: What you need from earlier units

sections.body:
The qsim project has 2,103 tests and all of them pass. That shows that no
bug those tests can see is present. Whether the tests can see the bugs that
matter is a separate question, and this unit is about answering it with
evidence instead of confidence.

A test can be blind in three ways: it checks the code against **itself**
(two copies of the same mistake agree), it checks a property the bug
**preserves** (a flipped measurement outcome on a state with `P(1) = 1/2`),
or it **cannot fail** (a comparison whose tolerance or sign pattern makes
any answer pass). The five layers of the next sections each close some of
these gaps and leave others open.

choices: The simulator is correct
No bug the tests can see is present; others may be
The tests are complete enough to stop adding new ones
questions.explain: Passing tests rule out the bugs they can detect. Whether they detect a particular kind of bug is measured separately: by injecting that bug (mutation testing, section 5) and checking that some test fails.
misconceptions: Tests can only refute; a passing suite is evidence against the bugs it can see. A flipped measurement outcome passed every frequency test on `|+⟩`, as section 6 shows.
How many tests there are says little about which bugs they see. Completeness is measured by injected bugs that a suite fails to kill, not by its size.
questions.prompt: All 2,103 tests of a simulator pass. Which conclusion is justified?

sections.title: The question: every test passes; how do you know the simulator is right?

analogies.breaks:
Both checks share the column of figures: a wrongly copied figure passes
both, as a wrong gate matrix passes the kernel-vs-`kron` check. And casting
out nines misses a swap of two digits, as a theory check misses a bug that
keeps the closed-form quantity unchanged. In both cases the fix is a check
that does not share the blind spot.
analogies.text:
An accountant adds a column twice, once top to bottom and once bottom to
top (layer 1), and checks the digit sum against the total's digit sum
(layer 2). The first catches a slip in one pass; the second catches a slip
in both passes that changes the digit sum.
analogies.title: Checking a sum by adding it twice, and by casting out nines

sections.body:
**Layer 1: redundant implementations.** Compute the same thing two
independent ways and compare. The bit-indexed kernel `apply_1q!` and the
dense matrix `kron(I, …, U, …, I)` share no code beyond the 2 × 2 gate
matrix, so a wrong index, a wrong stride or the wrong qubit order shows up
as a disagreement. The kernel and the FFT of unit 57 were both checked this
way. What this layer cannot see is a mistake in what both copies use: a
wrong gate matrix gives two identical wrong answers.

**Layer 2: theory checks.** Compare with a closed form derived on paper:
`P(0) = cos²(θ/2)` for `RY`, `S = 2√2` for CHSH, `sin²((2k + 1)θ)` for
Grover, the outcome distribution of phase estimation, `S = 2√2 (1 - p)` under
depolarising noise. A wrong gate matrix fails these. What this layer
cannot see is anything without a closed form, such as a random circuit.

Both layers need their tolerance derived, not tuned: a check that passes
because its tolerance was widened until it did has stopped being a check.

diagrams.alt: Five stacked boxes, one per layer of evidence, each with what it catches and what it cannot see. 1, redundant implementations: catches the kernel disagreeing with the dense kron; cannot see a wrong gate matrix both use. 2, theory checks: catches deviations from cos squared, sin squared of 2k plus 1 theta, and 2 root 2; cannot see anything with no closed form. 3, independent reference: Qiskit catches 17 of 22 mutants; cannot see sampling, measurement and partial trace. 4, controls that must fail: classical S = 2 and the product-state energy -1.25; catches a check that cannot fail. 5, mutation testing: 22 seeded bugs, all killed; cannot see bugs unlike any mutant.
diagrams.caption: Each layer has a blind spot, and another layer covers it. The Qiskit numbers are from `projects/qsim/README.md` (measured with `mutant_layers.py`, 100 random circuits per layer).

examples.caption: Layer 1: the bit-indexed kernel against the dense `kron` matrix on 200 random gates, states and qubits; then a mistake shared by both (a wrong `RY`), which this layer cannot see but a theory check does.
examples.code:
using Random
function apply_1q!(ψ, U, q)
    s = 1 << q
    for k in 0:length(ψ)-1
        if k & s == 0
            a, b = ψ[k + 1], ψ[k + s + 1]
            ψ[k + 1], ψ[k + s + 1] = U[1, 1] * a + U[1, 2] * b, U[2, 1] * a + U[2, 2] * b
        end
    end
    return ψ
end
I2 = ComplexF64[1 0; 0 1]
dense(U, q, n) = reduce(kron, [j == q ? U : I2 for j in n-1:-1:0])     # qubit 0 is the rightmost factor
rng = Xoshiro(61)
worst = 0.0
for _ in 1:200
    n = rand(rng, 1:5); q = rand(rng, 0:n-1)
    U = randn(rng, ComplexF64, 2, 2); ψ = randn(rng, ComplexF64, 2^n)
    worst = max(worst, maximum(abs.(apply_1q!(copy(ψ), U, q) - dense(U, q, n) * ψ)))
end
println("kernel vs dense, 200 cases, below 1e-13: ", worst < 1e-13)
RYbad(θ) = ComplexF64[cos(θ) -sin(θ); sin(θ) cos(θ)]        # full angle: a mistake both copies would use
ψ = ComplexF64[1, 0, 0, 0]
same = maximum(abs.(apply_1q!(copy(ψ), RYbad(0.7), 1) - dense(RYbad(0.7), 1, 2) * ψ))
println("with the wrong RY, kernel and dense still agree: ", same < 1e-15)
p0 = abs2(apply_1q!(copy(ψ), RYbad(0.7), 1)[1])
println("theory check P(0) = cos²(θ/2): ", round(p0; digits = 4), " vs ", round(cos(0.35)^2; digits = 4))
examples.output:
kernel vs dense, 200 cases, below 1e-13: true
with the wrong RY, kernel and dense still agree: true
theory check P(0) = cos²(θ/2): 0.585 vs 0.8824

sections.title: Layers 1 and 2: redundant implementations and theory checks

sections.body:
**Layer 3** compares with a simulator written by other people:
`projects/qsim/crosscheck/` runs 500 seeded random circuits through qsim,
through Qiskit (Javadi-Abhari et al.) and through Yao, amplitude for
amplitude up to a global phase, tolerance `1e-10`. Its measured record
against the 22 seeded bugs of `mutants.toml` (in `projects/qsim/README.md`):

* Qiskit caught 17, Yao 12. All 12 bugs in gates and gate application were
  caught by both.
* Yao's comparison caught **none** of the four QFT and phase-estimation
  bugs (only a guard that notices a changed circuit flagged them). Those are
  bugs in a circuit *builder*: qsim builds the wrong gate list, hands that
  same list to Yao, and both simulate it correctly. They agree. Qiskit
  caught them only because the diff compares against Qiskit's own library
  QFT and phase estimation, an independent algorithm, not just an
  independent simulator.
* Neither caught the sampler, measurement, partial-trace or Bloch-vector
  bugs, because neither diff looks at them. Only qsim's own tests did.

An independent reference also has conventions of its own. Qiskit's
`phase_estimation` returns its readout register with the bits in reversed
order (measured in `qiskit_diff.py`, which undoes it explicitly and checks
that skipping the undo fails). A diff that forgets the reversal reports a
mismatch, and someone who then "fixes" qsim to match has added a bug.

examples.caption: Reversing the bits of a `t`-bit readout: which outcomes are unchanged, so that a diff that forgets the reversal still agrees on them?
examples.code:
rev(k, t) = foldl((acc, i) -> acc | (((k >> i) & 1) << (t - 1 - i)), 0:t-1; init = 0)
println("t = 3: ", join(["$k→$(rev(k, 3))" for k in 0:7], "  "))
for t in (1, 3, 6, 8)
    same = count(k -> rev(k, t) == k, 0:2^t-1)
    println("t = $t: outcomes unchanged by the reversal: $same of $(2^t)")
end
examples.output:
t = 3: 0→0  1→4  2→2  3→6  4→1  5→5  6→3  7→7
t = 1: outcomes unchanged by the reversal: 2 of 2
t = 3: outcomes unchanged by the reversal: 4 of 8
t = 6: outcomes unchanged by the reversal: 8 of 64
t = 8: outcomes unchanged by the reversal: 16 of 256

choices: None
4 of 8
7 of 8
predict.explain: The unchanged outcomes are the bit palindromes: 000, 010, 101, 111. A diff tried only on `φ = 0`, `1/4`, `5/8` or `7/8` passes and hides the convention; with 6 or 8 bits, only 8 of 64 or 16 of 256 agree, so a larger test exposes it at once.
predict.prompt: A diff tests phase estimation with `t = 3` on all 8 exact phases `j/8` and forgets to undo the bit reversal. Before the output is shown: on how many of the 8 does it still agree?

choices: The tolerance of 1e-10 was too loose
Both simulated the same wrong gate list
Yao has no QFT gate in its block library at all
questions.explain: The builder is upstream of both simulators: the wrong circuit was simulated correctly by each, so they agreed. Comparing against an independently built QFT (Qiskit's `QFTGate`, or the DFT matrix of unit 57) catches it.
misconceptions: A wrong controlled-phase angle changes amplitudes by far more than `1e-10`. The comparison did not see a difference because there was none: both ran the same circuit.
Whether Yao has a library QFT does not matter here: the diff sends Yao qsim's gate list, so Yao never builds a QFT of its own.
questions.prompt: Yao and qsim agreed on every random circuit while qsim's QFT builder had a wrong angle. Why did the comparison not catch it?

sections.title: Layer 3: an independent reference, and what it shares with you

sections.body:
A **control** is a run where the check is expected to fail, or to give a
known different answer. It shows that the check can fail at all. Units
53 to 60 use several: the 16 classical CHSH strategies reach only 2;
teleportation without Bob's corrections has mean fidelity 1/2; the
variational circuit without its CNOT stops at -1.25.

The CHSH combination is `S = E(a,b) + E(a,b') + E(a',b) - E(a',b')`, and
which term carries the minus sign must match the angle choice. With
`a = 0`, `a' = π/2`, `b = π/4`, `b' = -π/4`, the three terms with a plus
are `cos(±π/4) = 1/√2` and the fourth is `cos(3π/4) = -1/√2`, so the minus
turns it into a fourth `+1/√2`. Put the minus on any other term and the
four contributions cancel.

A check `S ≤ 2√2 + 1e-12` (Cirel'son's bound) passes either way, since
`0 ≤ 2√2`. A check `S ≈ 2√2` fails on the wrong pattern, and the
classical control `S_classical == 2` confirms the combination itself.

examples.caption: The CHSH sum for the Bell state with the minus sign on each of the four terms in turn.
examples.code:
E(x, y) = cos(x - y)                  # the Bell-state correlator of unit 53
a, a′, b, b′ = 0.0, π/2, π/4, -π/4
terms = [E(a, b), E(a, b′), E(a′, b), E(a′, b′)]
for m in 1:4
    signs = [i == m ? -1 : 1 for i in 1:4]
    S = sum(signs .* terms)
    println("minus on term $m: S = ", round(S; digits = 4), ",  passes S ≤ 2√2: ", S <= 2sqrt(2) + 1e-12,
            ",  passes S ≈ 2√2: ", abs(S - 2sqrt(2)) < 1e-12)
end
examples.output:
minus on term 1: S = 0.0,  passes S ≤ 2√2: true,  passes S ≈ 2√2: false
minus on term 2: S = 0.0,  passes S ≤ 2√2: true,  passes S ≈ 2√2: false
minus on term 3: S = 0.0,  passes S ≤ 2√2: true,  passes S ≈ 2√2: false
minus on term 4: S = 2.8284,  passes S ≤ 2√2: true,  passes S ≈ 2√2: true

choices: About 1.41
About -2.83
predict.explain: Three terms are `+1/√2` and term 4 is `-1/√2`. With the minus on term 1 and not on term 4, the sum is `(-1 + 1 + 1 - 1)/√2 = 0`. The bound check `S ≤ 2√2` passes anyway; only the equality check and the classical control catch it.
predict.prompt: The minus sign belongs on term 4. Before the output is shown: what is S with the minus on term 1 instead?

choices: Nothing: 0 passes it
It fails, flagging the misplaced sign
It passes, so the state is entangled, as the bound requires
questions.explain: An upper bound cannot catch an answer that is too small. A check needs a way to fail on the bug in question: here the equality `S ≈ 2√2`, and the classical control `S = 2` that confirms the combination.
misconceptions: `0 ≤ 2√2`, so the bound holds and the check passes; it can only fail when S is too large.
Satisfying Cirel'son's bound says nothing about entanglement: every classical strategy satisfies it too. Entanglement is shown by exceeding 2.
questions.prompt: A CHSH test computes S = 0 because of a misplaced minus sign. What does the check `S ≤ 2√2 + 1e-12` tell you?

sections.title: Layer 4: controls that must fail; the CHSH sign pattern

sections.body:
**Mutation testing** (DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward) measures a test suite
instead of the program: inject one small bug (a **mutant**), run the
suite, and count the mutant as **killed** if some test fails (or the code
throws). The fraction killed is the **mutation score**. A surviving mutant
is either a bug the suite cannot see, which needs a new test, or an
**equivalent mutant** that does not change behaviour at all (unit 57's
inverse QFT that negates the phases without reversing the order is one).
qsim's suite kills all 22 seeded mutants of `mutants.toml`.

One mutant drew outcome 1 with probability `1 - P(1)` instead of `P(1)`,
and collapsed the state consistently with what it reported.
Every test on `|+⟩` passed: with `P(1) = 1/2`, reporting `1 - outcome` has
the same distribution. Teleportation (unit 54) measures only such qubits,
so it passed too. A frequency test on a lopsided state, `P(1) = 0.9`,
killed it.

Random **property** tests (Claessen and Hughes) generate many inputs, but a
property the bug preserves stays blind however many inputs it tries; the
lopsided state is a choice of input that breaks the symmetry.

examples.caption: Three mutants of `measure!` against two test suites: frequency on `|+⟩`, collapse (afterwards `P(1)` equals the outcome) and normalisation; then the same plus a frequency test with `P(1) = 0.9`. The reference must pass both.
examples.code:
using Random
function measure!(ψ, q, rng; bug = :none)
    s = 1 << q
    p1 = sum(abs2(ψ[k + 1]) for k in 0:length(ψ)-1 if k & s != 0)
    out = bug == :flip ? (rand(rng) < p1 ? 0 : 1) : (rand(rng) < p1 ? 1 : 0)   # the flip draws 1 with P = 1 - p1
    if bug != :nocollapse
        for k in 0:length(ψ)-1
            ((k & s != 0) != (out == 1)) && (ψ[k + 1] = 0)
        end
        bug != :nonorm && (ψ ./= sqrt(sum(abs2, ψ)))
    end
    return out
end
ry(p) = (θ = 2asin(sqrt(p)); ComplexF64[cos(θ/2), sin(θ/2)])           # a qubit with P(1) = p
function freq_test(bug, p)
    rng = Xoshiro(61); N = 20_000
    f = sum(measure!(ry(p), 0, rng; bug) for _ in 1:N) / N
    return abs(f - p) < 5sqrt(p * (1 - p) / N)
end
collapse_test(bug) = (rng = Xoshiro(62); all(begin ψ = ry(0.5); m = measure!(ψ, 0, rng; bug); abs(abs2(ψ[2]) - m) < 1e-12 end for _ in 1:200))
norm_test(bug) = (rng = Xoshiro(63); ψ = ry(0.5); measure!(ψ, 0, rng; bug); abs(sum(abs2, ψ) - 1) < 1e-12)
symmetric(bug) = freq_test(bug, 0.5) && collapse_test(bug) && norm_test(bug)
with_lopsided(bug) = symmetric(bug) && freq_test(bug, 0.9)
println("reference passes: ", symmetric(:none), ", ", with_lopsided(:none))
for (name, suite) in [("symmetric suite", symmetric), ("with the P(1) = 0.9 test", with_lopsided)]
    survivors = [m for m in (:flip, :nocollapse, :nonorm) if suite(m)]
    println(name, ": killed ", 3 - length(survivors), " of 3, survivors: ", isempty(survivors) ? "none" : join(survivors, ", "))
end

predict.explain: Without collapse, `P(1)` stays 1/2 after the measurement; without normalisation the norm is 1/2. Both fail a symmetric test. The flip keeps every property of a `P = 1/2` state, so only the lopsided frequency test sees it: the flip reports 1 with probability 0.1 instead of 0.9, hundreds of σ away.
predict.prompt: Before the output is shown: how many of the three mutants does the symmetric suite (all tests on `P(1) = 1/2`) kill?

choices: 20 000 shots are too few to resolve it
5σ is too wide a tolerance for this test
With P(1) = 1/2, the flipped outcome has the same distribution
questions.explain: Flipping a fair coin's reports gives a fair coin. No number of shots or tolerance can separate them; the input has to change, to a state where `P(1) ≠ 1/2`.
misconceptions: More shots would not help: the flipped sampler's frequency is exactly as close to 1/2 as the correct one's. At `P(1) = 0.9`, 20 000 shots separate them by hundreds of σ.
A tighter tolerance would make the correct sampler fail by chance more often, and still not separate the two, whose distributions are identical at `P = 1/2`.

sections.title: Layer 5: mutation testing; the measurement flip

sections.body:
Sampled checks have a power: a bug that shifts probabilities by `δ` is
seen only when `N` is large enough for `δ` to exceed a few `σ`. qsim's
`sampler-bias` mutant draws `rand()^1.05` instead of `rand()`; on the
distribution below that shifts the probabilities by +0.018, -0.003 and
-0.015. Pearson's statistic

```
χ² = Σ over outcomes of (O - N p)² / (N p)
```

compares observed counts `O` with the expected `N p`. For a correct
sampler with 3 outcomes it follows a chi-square distribution with 2
degrees of freedom, whose tail is `P(χ² > x) = exp(-x/2)`, so the
threshold `x = -2 ln(0.001) = 13.8` is exceeded by a correct sampler with
probability 0.001.

examples.caption: χ² of a correct and a biased sampler on the distribution (0.36, 0.2304, 0.4096), for three shot counts, against the 0.001 threshold 13.8.
examples.code:
using Random
p = [0.36, 0.2304, 0.4096]; cdf = cumsum(p)
chi2(c, p) = sum((c .- sum(c) .* p) .^ 2 ./ (sum(c) .* p))
for (name, draw) in [("correct", rng -> rand(rng)), ("biased ", rng -> rand(rng)^1.05)]
    for N in (1_000, 10_000, 100_000)
        rng = Xoshiro(61); c = zeros(Int, 3)
        for _ in 1:N
            c[min(searchsortedfirst(cdf, draw(rng)), 3)] += 1
        end
        x = chi2(c, p)
        println(name, "  N = ", lpad(N, 6), ":  χ² = ", lpad(round(x; digits = 1), 6), x > -2log(0.001) ? "  rejected" : "  passes")
    end
end

predict.explain: At `N = 10 000`, `σ` of a frequency near 0.36 is about 0.005, so the shifts are a few σ at most, and χ² = 7.3 stays below 13.8. At 100 000 shots `σ` is 0.0015 and χ² = 181. A check that passes says only that bugs larger than its resolution are absent.

sections.title: How many shots does a sampled check need?

units.summary: Five layers of evidence for a simulator: redundant implementations, closed-form theory checks, an independent reference, controls that must fail, and mutation testing. Three case studies: a CHSH sign pattern that gives S = 0, the bit reversal in Qiskit's phase_estimation readout, and a flipped measure! that passes a frequency test on |+⟩ and fails one on a lopsided state. A chi-square test on sampled counts misses a biased sampler at 10 000 shots and catches it at 100 000.
